implementation_notes: On the JVM the structure is a library class: GenericObjectPool<T> takes a PooledObjectFactory<T> whose makeObject/activateObject/passivateObject/validateObject/destroyObject hooks are exactly the pattern's create/reset/validate/destroy steps, borrowObject() hands a configured instance to a caller (blocking or failing per maxWait and blockWhenExhausted) and returnObject() takes it back. It also ships the operational parts people usually forget - maxTotal/maxIdle/minIdle bounds, an idle-object evictor, and abandoned-object tracking with logging for leases that are never returned. Without a library, an ArrayBlockingQueue<T> plus an init/reset callback in a finally block is the usual hand-rolled substitute.
pitfalls: A borrowed instance that is never returned is invisible until the pool starves: callers block on maxWait and time out - enable abandoned-object tracking or a lease timeout instead of assuming returnObject always runs.
Commons Pool will not guess your object's clean state: reset belongs in passivateObject (on return) or validation belongs in testOnBorrow (on borrow), otherwise the pool distributes dirty instances.

The pool class is thread-safe but the pooled objects are not - a borrowed connection or statement must be confined to one thread, and the evictor thread contends with callers, so aggressive eviction settings cost throughput.
